nameStory: Round-leaved dogwood gets its name from its distinctively rounded leaf tips, which set it apart from many of its pointy-leaved dogwood cousins. The 'dogwood' part of the name comes from an old English term 'dag wood,' referring to wood that was hard enough to make 'dags' or skewers. Some say it's because the wood was fit only for dogs, but the skewer story is more likely true!
description: Round-leaved dogwood is a small to medium-sized shrub or occasionally a small tree that typically grows 6-15 feet tall. It's a member of the dogwood family, featuring the classic dogwood traits of opposite leaves and small clustered flowers. This species has a somewhat open, irregular growth habit with multiple stems, and it's native to the cooler parts of eastern North America. Unlike the showy flowering dogwood with its big white bracts, this one produces small, creamy-white flowers in flat-topped clusters.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: The leaves are oval with distinctly rounded tips (not pointed like most dogwoods), measuring 2-4 inches long with prominent curved veins that follow the leaf's outline. Feel the leaf surface - it's noticeably rough and sandpapery on top, which matches its scientific name 'rugosa' meaning wrinkled or rough.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small creamy-white flowers appear in flat-topped clusters about 2-3 inches across in late spring to early summer. Each tiny flower has four petals and gives off a subtle, sweet fragrance when you get close.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Blue to blue-black berries ripen in late summer, each about the size of a small pea. They're arranged in loose clusters and have a whitish bloom (waxy coating) that rubs off easily when touched.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Young stems are green to reddish-brown and smooth, while older bark becomes grayish with shallow furrows. The bark has a slightly bitter smell when scratched with a fingernail.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms an open, somewhat irregular shrub with multiple stems arching outward from the base. Branches tend to grow in a loose, spreading pattern rather than densely upright.

habitat: Round-leaved dogwood thrives in cool, moist woodlands and forest edges, particularly in northern New England's mountains and cooler valleys. You'll often find it growing alongside sugar maples, yellow birch, and other northern hardwoods in rich, well-drained soils. It prefers partial shade and is especially common in areas that stay cool and humid during summer.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge with a reddish tinge before turning green, and the rough leaf texture becomes apparent as leaves fully expand.
seasonality.summer: Creamy-white flower clusters bloom in early summer, followed by developing green berries that gradually turn blue-black by late summer.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn beautiful shades of red to purple-red before dropping, while ripe blue-black berries persist and attract birds.
seasonality.winter: Bare stems show reddish-brown to gray bark, and the multiple-stemmed, spreading growth form becomes clearly visible against the snow.

funFact: The rough, sandpapery leaves of round-leaved dogwood were traditionally used by woodworkers as a natural sandpaper for smoothing and polishing wooden objects - nature's own abrasive!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with gray dogwood, but round-leaved dogwood's leaves have distinctly rounded (not pointed) tips and feel noticeably rougher to the touch. Memory trick: 'Round and rough' - both the leaf tips and texture help identify this species.
contextualKnowledge: Some botanists now place this species in the genus Swida rather than Cornus, reflecting new understanding of dogwood relationships. However, most field guides still use the traditional Cornus classification, so don't be surprised to see both names in different sources.
compareHints: Among New England dogwoods, round-leaved dogwood is unique for its combination of rounded leaf tips and rough leaf texture. Gray dogwood has pointed leaves and smooth bark, while red osier dogwood prefers wetter sites and has bright red winter stems. Silky dogwood also likes wet areas and has silky-hairy leaf undersides, unlike the rough-topped leaves of round-leaved dogwood.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its tree and shrub dogwood relatives, Canadian bunchberry is the only dogwood in New England that grows as a tiny herbaceous perennial on the forest floor.
Among dogwoods, this is the only one in New England with alternate leaves - all others have opposite leaves.
Among New England's dogwoods, red osier is the wetland specialist with the most colorful bark.
Among New England's dogwoods, silky dogwood is unique for its distinctly fuzzy leaf undersides - run your finger underneath any dogwood leaf, and only silky dogwood will feel soft and velvety.
Among New England's dogwoods, flowering dogwood is unique for its large, showy white bracts and tree-like size.

Among New England's dogwoods, gray dogwood is unique for its white berries on red stems - flowering dogwood has red berries, red osier dogwood has white berries on white stems, and silky dogwood has blue berries.
Among dogwoods, kousa is unique for its late bloom time, pointed bracts, and strawberry-like fruits.

Among New England dogwoods, blue-fruited dogwood is distinguished by its true blue berries - red osier dogwood has white berries, gray dogwood has white berries on red stems, and silky dogwood has blue-white berries.
Unlike our native flowering dogwood with its large white bracts, cornelian cherry has tiny yellow flowers in clusters.
Among New England dogwoods, roughleaf dogwood is unique for its sandpaper-textured leaves - no other dogwood species in our region has this distinctive rough feel.
Common dogwood stands out from other New England dogwoods primarily by its intensely colored winter stems - most of our native dogwoods have gray, brown, or only mildly reddish winter bark.

Among dogwoods, Tatarian dogwood's red stems are most similar to native red osier dogwood, but Tatarian tends to have more orange-red coloring and is found in drier garden settings rather than wetlands.

Korean cornel dogwood differs from most other dogwoods in New England by blooming very early with small yellow flowers rather than white ones, and by producing oval red fruits rather than round blue or white berries.
